column3: definition
The recurring organization of musical beats into groups, usually represented by a time signature and patterns of strong and weak beats.
A meter in which each main beat normally divides into two equal parts, as in 2/4, 3/4, or 4/4.
A time signature with two quarter-note beats per bar, often heard in marches, polkas, and other duple-meter music.
A time signature with three quarter-note beats per bar, commonly associated with waltzes and other triple-meter music.
A time signature with four quarter-note beats per bar, widely used in popular music and also called common time.
A meter in which each main beat normally divides into three equal parts, as in 6/8, 9/8, or 12/8.
A time signature usually felt as two dotted-quarter-note beats per bar, each divided into three eighth notes.
A time signature containing nine eighth notes per bar, usually grouped into three beats but sometimes organized asymmetrically.
A time signature usually felt as four dotted-quarter-note beats per bar, each divided into three eighth notes.
A meter whose subdivisions form unequal beat groups, such as 2+3 or 2+2+3, rather than a regular duple or triple pattern.
A time signature containing five quarter notes per bar, often grouped as three plus two or two plus three.
A time signature containing five eighth notes per bar, commonly grouped as two plus three or three plus two.
A time signature containing seven eighth notes per bar, commonly arranged in unequal groups such as 2+2+3.
A time signature containing seven quarter notes per bar, often grouped into smaller units such as four plus three.
A time signature containing eleven eighth notes per bar, typically organized into unequal groups of two and three.
A time signature containing thirteen eighth notes per bar, typically organized into an asymmetrical sequence of smaller beat groups.
An asymmetrical rhythmic organization built from unequal short and long beat units, particularly associated with Turkish and Balkan traditions.
The use of changing time signatures within a piece or passage, producing successive bars with different beat groupings.
Music without a consistently recurring metrical pattern; timing may instead follow melodic phrasing, text, or expressive needs.
A rhythmic or metrical effect in which a span normally grouped in twos is heard in threes, or vice versa, often creating a 3:2 relationship.
The simultaneous use of different metrical groupings in separate musical parts, often over a shared underlying pulse.
The perceived character of a rhythm, shaped by subdivision, accent, timing, and the placement of notes around the beat.
A rhythmic feel in which equal written subdivisions are performed with approximately equal durations rather than a swing pattern.
A rhythmic feel with unequal subdivisions and flexible timing, often giving paired eighth notes a long-short character.
A repeated long-short subdivision pattern, commonly based on triplets and widely used in blues, boogie-woogie, and related styles.
A rhythmic feel in which the beat is regularly divided into three parts, whether all three subdivisions are sounded or not.
A rhythmic feel that makes the music seem slower by placing major accents at half their usual rate without necessarily changing the tempo.
A rhythmic feel that makes the music seem faster by doubling the rate of prominent subdivisions or accents without necessarily changing the tempo.
A timing approach in which notes sit slightly behind the expected beat, creating a relaxed or spacious groove.
A rhythm with persistent forward momentum, created through strong pulse, repeated accents, or assertive placement of notes.
A compositional or performance technique that shapes rhythmic organization, accent, repetition, or the relationship between musical parts.
The emphasis of normally weak beats or subdivisions, or the displacement of accents away from the expected metrical pattern.
A note or chord sounded before its expected rhythmic or harmonic position, creating a sense of forward motion.
A beat or subdivision outside the main metrical accents, often emphasized to create rhythmic contrast or syncopation.
A strong accent on the second and fourth beats of a four-beat bar, commonly played on the snare drum in popular music.
The simultaneous use of contrasting rhythmic divisions, such as three evenly spaced notes against two over the same duration.
A polyrhythm in which three evenly spaced events occur against two evenly spaced events within the same time span.
A polyrhythm in which four evenly spaced events occur against three evenly spaced events within the same time span.
A sustained rhythmic relationship in which one pattern conflicts with the main beat grouping, often serving as a structural feature.
A recurring guide pattern that organizes rhythmic relationships in Afro-Cuban music, commonly expressed as five strokes across two measures.
A five-stroke Afro-Cuban clave pattern with three strokes in one measure and two in the other, played in either 3-2 or 2-3 orientation.
An Afro-Cuban clave pattern related to son clave, with a different placement of the final stroke on its three-stroke side.
A two-measure rhythmic pattern used in some bossa nova accompaniment, related to clave but not universally required by the style.
A three-attack rhythm often represented as 3+3+2 subdivisions within an eight-unit cycle, common in Afro-Latin music and popular styles.
A characteristic four-attack rhythm, commonly represented as 3+1+2+2 subdivisions, associated with the habanera and related dance traditions.
An accompaniment pattern of isolated ensemble accents separated by silence, leaving space for a singer or soloist.
The shifting of a rhythmic figure to a different position relative to the beat while preserving its internal pattern.
A tempo change established through a proportional relationship between rhythmic values in the old and new tempos.
One or more pickup notes that precede the first strong beat of a phrase or complete measure.
Short, coordinated accents played by several instruments together to emphasize a rhythmic point or transition.
The speed of the musical pulse, usually indicated by a verbal marking or a number of beats per minute.
A very slow musical pulse; Soundlore uses roughly below 60 BPM as a descriptive guide rather than a universal boundary.
A slow musical pulse; Soundlore uses roughly 60-80 BPM as a descriptive guide, with perceived speed also depending on meter and subdivision.
A moderate musical pulse; Soundlore uses roughly 85-110 BPM as a descriptive guide rather than a fixed musical category.
A fast musical pulse; Soundlore uses roughly 115-150 BPM as a descriptive guide, with perceived speed varying by musical context.
A very fast musical pulse; Soundlore uses roughly above 160 BPM as a descriptive guide rather than a universal boundary.
A change in the speed of the musical pulse, either gradual or sudden, within a piece or passage.
A gradual increase in tempo, making the musical pulse progressively faster.
A gradual decrease in tempo, often used to relax a phrase or prepare a musical ending.
Expressive flexibility in timing, allowing notes or phrases to stretch and compress around the underlying pulse.
A notation indicating that a note, chord, or rest should be held longer than its written duration.
An abrupt change from one tempo to another, usually at a section boundary or other clear structural point.
A recurring arrangement of drum or percussion sounds that establishes a groove, rhythmic feel, or stylistic identity.
A common rock groove combining a steady cymbal subdivision with kick-drum support and snare accents on beats two and four.
A drum pattern with a kick-drum hit on every quarter-note beat in 4/4, especially common in disco, house, and dance music.
A percussion groove built from emphatic foot-stomp or kick-like sounds alternating with handclaps.
A drum groove derived from or resembling a percussion break, often syncopated and used as a sampled or programmed rhythmic foundation.
The widely sampled drum break from the Winstons' recording of "Amen, Brother", influential in jungle, drum and bass, and other electronic styles.
Sampled drum breaks cut into smaller fragments and rearranged to create new rhythms, accents, or rapid variations.
A syncopated garage-style groove that omits some regular four-on-the-floor kick hits while retaining a strong dance pulse.
A hip-hop production and drum style emphasizing prominent kick and snare sounds, often built from sampled breaks.
A programmed groove typically combining deep 808-style bass, a sparse snare or clap pattern, and rapid or rolling hi-hats.
Rapid hi-hat patterns using rolls, short subdivisions, and triplets to add movement and detail to trap-style beats.
A drill-style groove often featuring displaced snare accents, syncopated hi-hats, and sliding bass, with regional variations.
A repeating rhythmic pattern central to reggaeton and related styles, rooted in dancehall and characterized by a syncopated kick-and-snare relationship.
A reggae drum pattern emphasizing the third beat of a four-beat bar while typically leaving the first beat without a kick accent.
A reggae drum pattern with a kick on each quarter-note beat, often combined with offbeat accompaniment and dub production.
A reggae drum approach with more active kick patterns than one drop, supporting a steady groove and syncopated accompaniment.
A fast punk drum pattern associated with Discharge, defined by a driving, asymmetrical kick-and-snare cycle.
A fast drum pattern that alternates kick and snare accents, commonly used in punk and extreme metal.
A very rapid drum pattern combining repeated snare, kick, and cymbal strokes, commonly heard in grindcore and extreme metal.
Drumming that uses two bass drums or a double pedal to produce rapid, repeated, or interlocking kick-drum strokes.
A repeated rhythmic figure commonly played as an eighth note followed by two sixteenth notes, especially on guitar or bass drum.
A steady, repetitive 4/4 drum groove with persistent forward motion, strongly associated with krautrock.
A snare-driven groove whose repeated accents suggest the motion of a train, common in country and rockabilly.
A half-time shuffle associated with Bernard Purdie, combining a strong backbeat with shuffled subdivisions and quiet ghost notes.
A New Orleans parade-derived rhythmic feel with syncopated accents, layered percussion, and a buoyant marching groove.
A restrained Brazilian groove combining bass accents and syncopated upper voices or percussion, often adapted from samba accompaniment.
An interlocking samba percussion groove in which low drum pulses support syncopated patterns played by higher-pitched instruments.
A northeastern Brazilian dance rhythm commonly articulated by zabumba, triangle, and other instruments in a syncopated duple groove.
A cumbia groove built from a repeating duple pulse and interlocking percussion patterns, with instrumentation varying by region.
A repeating syncopated accompaniment pattern, especially for bass or congas, used in Cuban music and salsa.
Layered, syncopated drumming that combines funk-like grooves with West African rhythmic approaches, closely associated with Afrobeat.
A fast club groove using distinctive clustered kick patterns, chopped vocals, and repeated samples associated with Jersey club.
A fast, highly syncopated electronic groove, often around 160 BPM, designed for footwork dance and rapid rhythmic interplay.
A reusable instrumental backing track or rhythmic foundation over which multiple dancehall performers can record different songs.
A percussion pattern associated with Brazilian funk carioca, combining repeated low and high drum sounds in a syncopated groove.
A rhythmic bass pattern built from the pitched, percussive log-drum sound associated with amapiano production.
A method of playing drums or percussion that shapes articulation, sound, coordination, or rhythmic complexity.
Very quiet drum strokes placed between stronger accents to add movement, texture, and rhythmic nuance.
A short drum phrase that interrupts or embellishes the main groove, often leading into a new section.
A rapid succession of drum strokes that creates a sustained or nearly continuous sound.
A repeated snare pattern that becomes denser, faster, or louder to build tension before a transition or drop.
A drum rudiment consisting of a soft grace stroke immediately followed by a stronger stroke, producing a thickened attack.
A drumming technique in which a stick rests across the drumhead and strikes the rim, producing a short, woody click.
A production or arrangement descriptor for repetitive tom-drum patterns with a strong percussive pulse; it does not identify a specific cultural tradition.
A passage in which drums become the principal musical focus, often highlighting rhythmic invention and performance technique.
A drumming approach in which successive notes are distributed across instruments without simultaneous strikes.
A percussion technique using brushes instead of regular sticks to produce softer taps, swishes, and continuous textured sounds.
The organization of musical pitches around a central note or chord, with relationships that create stability, motion, and resolution.
A tonal organization centered on a major tonic chord and major-scale relationships; its expressive character depends on context.
A tonal organization centered on a minor tonic chord, often drawing on natural, harmonic, and melodic minor resources.
The use of a mode as a basis for melody or harmony, often without the dominant-to-tonic priorities of functional major-minor tonality.
Music that avoids establishing a stable tonal center or the conventional hierarchy of pitches found in tonal music.
The simultaneous use of two or more distinct tonal centers or keys in different musical layers.
The use of pitch intervals or tuning systems that differ from the standard twelve equal divisions of the octave.
A combination of pitches heard as a harmonic unit, sounded together or implied through successive notes.
A three-note chord consisting of a root, third, and fifth, conventionally described as major, minor, diminished, or augmented.
A chord voicing built mainly from a root and perfect fifth, often doubled at the octave and lacking a third.
A chord formed from a triad plus a seventh above its root, creating several common major, minor, and dominant types.
A chord combining a major triad with a major seventh above the root.
A chord combining a minor triad with a minor seventh above the root.
A chord combining a major triad with a minor seventh, often used to create harmonic tension or a blues color.
A chord combining a diminished triad with a minor seventh, also written as a minor seventh chord with a flattened fifth.
A chord that includes or implies tones beyond the seventh, such as ninths, elevenths, or thirteenths.
A chord in which the third is replaced by a second or fourth, producing a sound that can suggest delayed resolution.
A chord with an added color tone, such as a second, sixth, or ninth, without necessarily including a seventh.
A chord built around a minor third and diminished fifth, sometimes extended with further minor thirds.
A triad consisting of a root, major third, and augmented fifth, dividing the octave into equal major-third intervals.
A chord containing chromatically modified tones, commonly altered fifths or ninths in dominant harmony.
A chord symbol that specifies a bass note after a slash, which may be a chord tone or an independent added pitch.
Harmony constructed mainly from stacked fourths rather than the thirds typical of triadic harmony.
A dense chord formed from closely adjacent pitches, often producing a compact, dissonant sound mass.
A major chord built on the lowered second scale degree, commonly used in first inversion before a dominant harmony.
A compositional technique that shapes chord relationships, harmonic color, voice leading, or tonal tension.
The use of chords or pitches borrowed from a parallel mode, such as minor-mode harmonies within a major-key passage.
A dominant-function chord that temporarily points toward a chord other than the main tonic.
The replacement of a dominant seventh chord by another dominant seventh chord whose root lies a tritone away.
A chromatic relationship between chords or tonal centers a major or minor third apart, often involving notes outside the prevailing key.
A major tonic chord used at the end of a passage or piece otherwise set in a minor key or mode.
An interval spanning three whole tones, equivalent in equal temperament to an augmented fourth or diminished fifth.
A relationship between pitches that creates perceived tension or instability, with its meaning depending on musical style and context.
A sustained or repeated pitch that remains in one part while the surrounding harmonies change.
The replacement or modification of chords supporting a melody while retaining much of the melodic material.
The rate and pattern at which harmonies change within a musical passage.
Harmonic practices associated with jazz, including extended chords, chromatic voice leading, substitutions, and flexible treatment of dissonance.
A brief chord used to connect more stable harmonies through smooth bass movement or voice leading.
A bass line that descends through semitone steps, often supporting changing harmonies or a sustained upper structure.
A familiar voice-leading pattern in which one note moves chromatically while much of the surrounding harmony stays fixed.
An ordered sequence of chords that provides harmonic movement and structure within a piece or passage.
A four-chord major-key progression moving from tonic to dominant, relative minor, and subdominant, widely used in popular music.
A progression moving from tonic to relative minor, subdominant, and dominant, strongly associated with doo-wop and early popular music.
A progression from the supertonic chord through the dominant to the tonic, central to much jazz harmony.
A twelve-measure blues framework organized around tonic, subdominant, and dominant harmonies, with many rhythmic and harmonic variants.
A descending four-chord pattern commonly represented as i-bVII-bVI-V in a minor-key interpretation, associated with flamenco and other styles.
A chord sequence whose roots move mainly by descending fifths or ascending fourths, often creating a strong sense of harmonic direction.
The eight-chord sequence associated with Pachelbel's Canon, commonly represented in major keys as I-V-vi-iii-IV-I-IV-V.
A progression commonly represented as IV-V-iii-vi in a major key, associated with Japanese popular music and anime songs.
A minor-key four-chord loop moving i-VI-III-VII, often used for broad, dramatic effects in rock, electronic music, and soundtrack-style arrangements.
A repeating I-bVII-IV chord pattern that draws on Mixolydian-scale relationships and is common in rock-oriented harmony.
A short musical phrase or chord pattern repeated for an extended period as accompaniment or a basis for improvisation.
A passage whose harmonic foundation remains on one chord, with interest supplied by rhythm, melody, timbre, or changing voicings.
A movement from the minor subdominant to a major tonic, producing a characteristic borrowed-chord resolution.
A melodic or harmonic gesture that marks a point of arrival, pause, or closure in a musical phrase.
A cadence moving from dominant harmony to tonic harmony, with its strength depending on voicing, melody, and metric placement.
A cadence moving from subdominant harmony to tonic harmony, often described as an IV-I or "Amen" close.
A phrase ending on dominant harmony, usually creating an open or expectant sense rather than full resolution.
A cadence in which an expected dominant-to-tonic resolution is redirected to another chord, commonly the submediant.
A jazz-oriented resolution approaching the tonic through a dominant seventh chord on the flattened seventh scale degree, often preceded by iv.
A change from one tonal center or key to another within a piece or passage.
An abrupt upward key change, often by a semitone or whole tone near a final chorus, used to increase intensity.
A key change that uses a chord shared by the old and new keys as a connecting harmonic pivot.
A sudden change of key without a connecting pivot chord or extended harmonic preparation.
A change between major and minor keys that share the same tonic, such as C major and C minor.
An ordered collection of pitches used as a basis for melody, harmony, or musical organization.
A seven-note diatonic scale with the interval pattern whole-whole-half-whole-whole-whole-half from its tonic.
A seven-note scale with the interval pattern whole-half-whole-whole-half-whole-whole, equivalent to the Aeolian mode.
A minor scale with a raised seventh degree, creating a leading tone and an augmented second between the sixth and seventh degrees.
A minor scale conventionally using raised sixth and seventh degrees when ascending; jazz practice often retains this form in both directions.
A scale containing five distinct pitches within an octave, found in many musical traditions and several different interval patterns.
A five-note scale corresponding to degrees 1, 2, 3, 5, and 6 of the major scale.
A five-note scale corresponding to degrees 1, b3, 4, 5, and b7, widely used in blues and rock improvisation.
A scale commonly formed by adding a chromatic blue note to a pentatonic collection, with several major and minor variants.
A six-note scale in which each neighboring pitch is separated by a whole tone, producing a symmetrical pitch collection.
An eight-note symmetrical scale alternating whole tones and semitones, also called the diminished scale in jazz contexts.
A scale comprising all twelve semitone-separated pitch classes of the standard equal-tempered octave.
An eight-note scale created by adding a chromatic passing tone to a seven-note scale, often used to align chord tones with strong beats.
A seven-note scale used over altered dominant chords, equivalent to the seventh mode of the ascending melodic minor scale.
A pitch framework defined by its interval pattern and tonal center; in Western theory, modes often refer to rotations of a diatonic scale.
A minor-type diatonic mode with a major sixth and minor seventh, corresponding to 1, 2, b3, 4, 5, 6, b7.
A minor-type diatonic mode with a lowered second degree, corresponding to 1, b2, b3, 4, 5, b6, b7.
A major-type diatonic mode with a raised fourth degree, corresponding to 1, 2, 3, #4, 5, 6, 7.
A major-type diatonic mode with a lowered seventh degree, corresponding to 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, b7.
A diatonic mode with a lowered second and fifth, corresponding to 1, b2, b3, 4, b5, b6, b7.
A grouping for frameworks of particular musical traditions that organize pitch beyond a scale, through hierarchies of degrees, characteristic phrases, ornament, intonation or ensemble tuning.
A scale with degrees 1, b2, 3, 4, 5, b6, b7, equivalent to the fifth mode of harmonic minor.
A seven-note scale with lowered second and sixth degrees relative to major, producing two augmented-second intervals.
A minor scale with raised fourth and seventh degrees, corresponding to 1, 2, b3, #4, 5, b6, 7.
Scale resources associated with Japanese traditions, including several pentatonic patterns whose intervals and uses vary by repertory.
A modal framework in Arabic music governing pitch relationships, melodic movement, and expression; related systems also exist in neighboring traditions.
A melodic framework in Indian classical music defined by characteristic pitches, movements, phrases, and expressive conventions, rather than a scale alone.
The tuning systems of Indonesian gamelan, slendro and pelog, whose interval sizes vary from one ensemble to another.
A recognizable unit of melodic material, such as a motif, riff, or phrase, that helps shape a composition.
A memorable musical or lyrical idea designed to attract attention and remain recognizable after listening.
A short, recurring instrumental figure that provides rhythmic, melodic, or harmonic identity to a piece.
A brief musical idea that can be repeated, varied, or developed to help unify a composition.
A recurring musical idea associated with a character, place, object, or dramatic concept.
A musical pattern repeated persistently, often providing a stable foundation beneath changing material.
A secondary melodic line that complements or contrasts with the principal melody.
The principal vocal melody, often written together with lyrics over an existing instrumental backing track.
The notes of a chord played successively rather than simultaneously, often in an ascending or descending pattern.
The repetition of a melodic idea at a different pitch level, preserving much of its interval or rhythmic shape.
A technique used to shape, vary, decorate, or connect melodic material.
The use of pitches outside a prevailing diatonic scale, often involving semitone motion or altered harmonies.
A pitch inflection associated with blues expression, often involving flexible or lowered versions of the third, fifth, or seventh scale degree.
Decorative notes or gestures that embellish a melody without replacing its main structural pitches.
A rapid alternation between a principal note and a nearby pitch, usually a scale step above it.
A short ornament that moves from a principal note to a neighboring note and quickly returns.
A brief ornamental note whose timing is understood in relation to an adjacent principal note rather than as a fully independent rhythmic value.
An ornament that circles a principal pitch by visiting upper and lower neighboring notes.
A movement between pitches by sliding continuously or passing rapidly through intervening notes, depending on the instrument.
The singing of several notes on a single syllable of text.
A vocal setting in which each syllable is generally assigned one note rather than a sequence of notes.
Melodic movement mainly by neighboring scale steps rather than wide intervals.
Melodic movement characterized by leaps larger than a scale step.
The performance of the same melodic line at pitch levels one or more octaves apart.
The creation or substantial shaping of music during performance rather than following a completely fixed written part.
Improvisation organized around a mode or limited set of modal harmonies, allowing melodic exploration over relatively stable accompaniment.
An improvisational exchange in which performers alternate four-measure phrases, commonly between soloists and a drummer in jazz.
A distinct part of a song, identified by its musical material, lyrical role, or position within the arrangement.
An opening passage that establishes atmosphere, rhythm, or musical material before the main body of a piece.
A recurring song section whose music is often similar each time while its lyrics develop or change.
A section between verse and chorus that prepares the chorus through rising tension, contrasting material, or transitional harmony.
A recurring central section of a song, usually carrying its main hook and relatively stable lyrics.
A section immediately after the chorus that extends its energy or presents an additional hook.
A recurring line or musical passage, often returning within or at the end of successive verses.
A contrasting song section that departs from established verse or chorus material before returning to it.
A short passage inserted between larger sections, often instrumental or transitional in character.
A passage in which instruments take over while the principal vocal part pauses.
A passage that foregrounds one performer or instrument, often for melodic invention, improvisation, or technical display.
A passage featuring guitar as the principal melodic voice, whether improvised, composed, acoustic, or electric.
A passage in which saxophone takes the leading melodic role, often supported by a rhythm section or ensemble.
A passage featuring piano in the leading role, either unaccompanied or supported by other instruments.
A passage foregrounding a synthesizer lead, often using distinctive timbres, pitch bends, or melodic runs.
A passage featuring bass as the main musical voice, emphasizing melodic, rhythmic, or harmonic possibilities beyond accompaniment.
A heavy, rhythmically focused section in metal or hardcore, often using slower-feeling grooves, rests, and repeated low-register riffs.
A lower-intensity section in electronic dance music that reduces or removes the main beat before rebuilding energy.
A passage that increases tension through rising intensity, added layers, repetition, or denser rhythmic activity before a release.
A high-impact section in electronic dance music where the principal beat, bass, or hook enters or returns after a buildup or break.
A deliberate change of the underlying beat or production within a track, often marking a new section or expressive direction.
The recurring hook section of a hip-hop track, often functioning as a chorus between verses.
A brief spoken scene, comic passage, or narrative vignette included within a song or between tracks on an album.
A spoken opening that introduces a track, establishes a narrative, or sets an atmosphere before the main musical section.
The last occurrence of a song's chorus, often varied or intensified to provide a climactic finish.
A short harmonic passage that leads from the end of a section back to its beginning or into the next repetition.
A short ending extension that repeats or varies a final phrase, line, or chord pattern.
The closing section of a piece, providing a final statement, resolution, or gradual departure from the main material.
A recording or performance ending in which the sound level gradually decreases until it becomes inaudible.
A clear, abrupt ending achieved through a final note, chord, hit, or cutoff rather than a gradual fade.
A moment that appears to end the music before it resumes, creating surprise or renewed momentum.
A passage performed by voices without instrumental accompaniment, even if the surrounding music uses instruments.
A deliberate interruption of all sounding parts, used to create tension, emphasis, or a sharp structural contrast.
The overall organization of a song into repeated and contrasting sections, such as verses, choruses, and bridges.
A song structure built around alternating verses and recurring choruses, sometimes including an introduction, bridge, and outro.
A four-section form in which two related A sections are followed by a contrasting B section and a return of A.
A form that uses the same music for successive verses or stanzas of text.
A form in which new musical material follows the text or narrative instead of relying on a regularly repeating sectional pattern.
A musical form organized into two principal sections, often labeled A and B and commonly repeated.
A three-part form with an opening section, contrasting middle section, and return of the opening material.
A dance-oriented arrangement that organizes energy through introductions, buildups, drops, breakdowns, and an ending; exact sequences vary.
An extended composition joining several contrasting sections or movements into a larger continuous or linked work.
A structure created by repeating musical loops while adding, removing, or transforming layers over time.
A piece or performance that joins recognizable portions of several existing songs or compositions.
A return of previously heard musical material, often later in a composition, performance, or album.
A transition from one musical passage or track into another without a significant break.
A recognized framework or type of composition associated with particular structural, performance, or historical conventions.
A contrapuntal composition in which a principal subject enters successively in different voices and is developed through imitation.
A contrapuntal technique in which one part strictly follows another after a delay, sometimes at a different pitch level.
A repeating canon in which several performers begin the same melody at different times, usually at the same pitch level.
A short contrapuntal keyboard composition, commonly in two parts, that develops a small amount of musical material.
A large-scale form typically involving exposition, development, and recapitulation, with thematic and tonal contrasts shaping its design.
A form presenting a theme followed by successive versions that alter its melody, harmony, rhythm, texture, or instrumentation.
A composition built from continuing variations over a recurring bass line or harmonic pattern.
A form in which a recurring principal section alternates with contrasting episodes.
A composition emphasizing fluency, rapid passagework, or touch, most often associated with keyboard instruments.
A short introductory piece or an independent composition, often freely structured and designed to establish a musical mood.
A composition designed to develop or demonstrate a particular performance technique, sometimes also intended for concert presentation.
A composition associated with nighttime atmosphere, often lyrical and especially common in the piano repertory.
A composition with a regular walking or marching pulse, commonly in duple meter and often associated with ceremonial or military use.
A dance or composition in triple meter, typically with a strong first beat and lighter accompanying beats.
A courtly dance and musical form in triple meter, later used as a movement in instrumental works.
A lively, often playful or sharply contrasting movement, frequently in triple meter and commonly found in larger instrumental works.
A self-contained vocal piece for a solo singer, often expressing emotion within an opera, oratorio, or cantata.
A vocal style that follows the inflections and rhythm of speech to convey dialogue or advance a dramatic narrative.
A hymn tune associated with Protestant, especially Lutheran, worship, or a composition based on such a tune.
A vocal composition, often sacred and polyphonic, whose musical form and text conventions vary across historical periods.
A secular vocal composition, especially associated with Renaissance and early Baroque traditions, often using expressive musical treatment of poetry.
A musical setting of texts from the Christian Mass, especially its Ordinary, written for voices with or without instruments.
A musical setting of the Mass for the dead, or a composition inspired by its texts and memorial function.
A song of praise or devotion, commonly intended for communal singing in a religious setting.
A song or choral work serving a communal, ceremonial, religious, or symbolic purpose; the term has several historical meanings.
A gentle song or instrumental piece intended to soothe, especially to help a child fall asleep.
A musical expression of grief, mourning, loss, or complaint, found in many vocal and instrumental traditions.
A composition traditionally associated with evening performance or an affectionate address, later also used for multi-movement instrumental works.
A song type associated with storytelling or, in modern popular music, a lyrical and often slower-paced expression of emotion.
A popular-music ballad that develops from a restrained opening into an intense arrangement with prominent drums and amplified instruments.
A freely organized, often contrasting or episodic composition with an expressive or improvisatory character.
A composition with a free or imaginative structure, often drawing on improvisatory gestures or loosely connected musical ideas.
A featured solo passage, often virtuosic and rhythmically flexible, inserted into or near the close of a larger movement.
An instrumental opening to an opera, play, or other larger work, also used for independent concert pieces.
A collection of related movements or pieces presented as a larger work, historically often based on a sequence of dances.
A composition that features one or more soloists in a prominent relationship with an orchestra or other ensemble.
An extended orchestral composition, commonly organized into several movements with contrasting tempos and characters.
A vocal composition in several sections or movements, typically involving soloists, choir, and instrumental accompaniment.
A substantial dramatic work for voices and instruments, usually performed without the staging, costumes, or acting of an opera.
A theatrical work in which music and singing play a central role in presenting characters and drama, sometimes alongside spoken dialogue.
A composition widely recognized and repeatedly performed in the jazz repertory, often used as a framework for improvisation.
The way melodic, harmonic, and rhythmic parts combine, including their density, independence, and relationships.
A texture consisting of one melodic line without independent harmonic accompaniment, whether performed by one or several musicians.
A texture in which parts move together harmonically or a principal melody is supported by chordal accompaniment.
A texture containing two or more simultaneously sounding melodic parts with some degree of independence.
A texture in which performers simultaneously produce different versions or embellishments of the same underlying melody.
The simultaneous performance of the same pitch or melodic line by multiple voices or instruments.
A musical texture with relatively few simultaneous sounds, leaving audible space between or around its parts.
A musical texture containing many simultaneous or closely packed layers, voices, or events.
